title: Complete Guide to the Bauhaus Design Process
description: How the Bauhaus taught design: the Vorkurs, workshop training, form follows function, and a step-by-step look at the school's famous design process.
body_html:
The Bauhaus design process was a structured path from raw perception to finished product. Every student began with the Vorkurs, a preliminary course that stripped away habits and taught the fundamentals of material, color, and form. Only after passing it did students enter a specialized workshop — metal, furniture, weaving, typography, ceramics, or wall painting — where they learned a craft under two masters and designed objects intended for industrial production. The guiding conviction, often summarized as "form follows function," was that an object's shape should emerge from its purpose, its material, and the logic of how it would be made.

Founded by Walter Gropius in Weimar, Germany, in 1919, and later based in Dessau and briefly Berlin before closing under political pressure in 1933, the Bauhaus existed for only fourteen years. Yet its process — analyze the problem, study the material, prototype, refine for manufacture — became the template for modern design education worldwide. This guide walks through each stage of that process and shows how you can apply it, or recognize it, in buildings and objects today.

Why the Bauhaus Needed a New Process

Gropius founded the school by merging an academy of fine art with a school of applied arts, and his founding manifesto called for unifying art, craft, and technology. In the aftermath of the First World War, he argued that architects, painters, and craftspeople should work together toward the "building of the future" — a total work in which every discipline contributed. That ambition demanded a shared method: artists could no longer rely on academic drawing traditions, and craftspeople could no longer rely on inherited workshop habits. Everyone would start from first principles.

The result was a curriculum organized like a set of concentric rings. Students moved from the outer ring — the preliminary course — inward through material studies and workshop training, with building itself at the theoretical center. If you want to see where the school's own aesthetic landed, the Bauhaus style guide in our building library summarizes its hallmarks: flat roofs, ribbon windows, asymmetric composition, and an almost total absence of ornament.

Stage One: The Vorkurs (Preliminary Course)

The Vorkurs was the school's great pedagogical invention. Created by Johannes Itten and later reshaped by László Moholy-Nagy and Josef Albers, it was a mandatory foundation semester (later extended) that every student completed before choosing a workshop. Its purpose was twofold: unlearn academic conventions, and build direct, hands-on knowledge of how materials and forms behave.

Typical Vorkurs exercises included:

  • Material studies: cutting, folding, and combining paper, wood, wire, glass, and textiles to discover each material's structural character — what it can span, hold, or express.
  • Contrast studies: pairing opposites such as rough and smooth, light and dark, or geometric and organic to sharpen perception.
  • Basic form and color: exercises built around elementary forms (circle, square, triangle) and color theory, an area where Itten, Wassily Kandinsky, and Paul Klee all taught influential courses.
  • Economy of means: under Albers especially, producing the strongest possible result from a single sheet of paper or a minimal set of operations.

The Vorkurs treated creativity as trainable. Rather than asking "what should this look like?", students learned to ask "what does this material want to do, and what does this problem require?" — the question that drives the entire Bauhaus process.

Stage Two: Workshop Training Under Two Masters

After the Vorkurs, students entered a workshop and trained in a real craft. In the early Weimar years each workshop was led jointly by a Master of Form — an artist such as Kandinsky, Klee, or Moholy-Nagy responsible for aesthetic and theoretical direction — and a Master of Craft, a trained artisan responsible for technique. This dual-master system embodied the school's core belief: good design requires both artistic judgment and material competence, and neither can substitute for the other.

Workshops functioned as laboratories rather than classrooms. Students learned by making: joining wood, raising metal, dressing looms, setting type. Famous results include Marcel Breuer's tubular-steel furniture, Marianne Brandt's geometric metalwork for lighting and tableware, and the weaving workshop's textiles under figures such as Gunta Stölzl. As the school matured in Dessau, former students became "young masters" who led workshops themselves, and the artist/craftsman split gradually merged into a single teaching role.

Stage Three: Form Follows Function — the Design Logic

The functionalist logic applied in the workshops can be described as a repeatable sequence:

  1. Define the function. What must the object or building actually do? A teapot must pour cleanly; a chair must support the body; housing must deliver light, air, and economy.
  2. Analyze the user and context. Bauhaus designers studied how objects were used and how buildings were inhabited, aiming at broad social need rather than luxury commissions.
  3. Choose materials honestly. Steel, glass, concrete, and plywood were used for what they are, without disguise. Structure was expressed, not hidden behind ornament.
  4. Reduce to essentials. Decoration that did not serve function was removed. Geometry, proportion, and color did the expressive work.
  5. Prototype and test. Workshops built working models, criticized them collectively, and revised.
  6. Design for reproduction. The final step asked whether industry could manufacture the design affordably at scale.

The slogan "form follows function" predates the school — it is associated with the American architect Louis Sullivan — but the Bauhaus turned it from an aphorism into a working method.

Stage Four: From Prototype to Industry

Especially after the 1925 move to Dessau, Gropius reframed the school's mission as "art and technology — a new unity." Workshops were expected to produce prototypes that manufacturers could license, and royalties helped fund the school. Wallpaper, textiles, lamps, and furniture designs reached actual production, making the Bauhaus one of the first design schools to close the loop between studio and factory. Under later directors — Hannes Meyer, who pushed the school further toward scientific method and social housing, and finally Ludwig Mies van der Rohe — architecture itself became a formal department, completing the curriculum Gropius had sketched in 1919.

How to Apply the Bauhaus Process Today

You do not need a workshop in Dessau to design like the Bauhaus. Start any project — a renovation, a piece of furniture, even a webpage — by writing down its true function in one sentence. List the materials you intend to use and what each does best. Strip every element that does not serve the function, then ask whether what remains is beautiful in its proportions alone. Iterate physically where possible: rough models expose problems that drawings hide.

Training your eye is the other half. The Bauhaus survives in thousands of buildings, from the Dessau school building itself to countless mid-century schools, offices, and houses influenced by émigré teachers. If you spot a flat-roofed building with ribbon windows and want to know whether it carries Bauhaus DNA, upload a photo to our AI architecture explorer and it will identify the style and its telltale features. To see how the movement fits into the broader story of the continent that produced it, read our overview of European architectural styles.

The deepest lesson of the Bauhaus process is that design is not decoration applied at the end — it is a disciplined inquiry that begins with function, respects material, and ends only when nothing inessential remains.
